chief_complaint: electric shock pain in cheek triggered by light breeze
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with electric shock pain in cheek triggered by light breeze. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he might have a cracked molar or an infected nerve root shooting pain through his jaw.
concerns: He is worried that the excruciating shocks will become constant and prevent him from chewing food or speaking with clients.
expectations: He hopes to receive strong prescription pain medication to halt the shocks immediately and a referral to a specialist.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Trigeminal Neuralgia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Trigeminal Neuralgia: Carbamazepine, monitor CBC/LFTs/sodium, microvascular decompression, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Trigeminal Neuralgia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dental pathology without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Bilateral pain.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Microvascular compression of the trigeminal nerve causing electric shock pain in the cheek triggered by a light breeze.

must_ask.say: Does the pain feel like an electric shock?
Does wind or touch trigger it?
How long does each episode last?

history.answer: Doctor, I've been having this unbearable electric shock pain in my right cheek whenever a light breeze touches my face.
It started about two weeks ago out of nowhere, and the attacks have become more frequent and intense since then.
The pain strikes specifically on the right side of my cheek, right next to my nose and upper jaw. It does not spread to my forehead or neck.
It feels like an intense, stabbing jolt of electricity shooting across my face.
During an attack, it is a ten out of ten. It is so excruciating that I freeze completely.
Each shock lasts just a couple of seconds, never more than a minute at a time.
Yes, between the attacks the pain goes away completely, and my cheek feels normal.
At first it happened once or twice a day, but now it happens dozens of times a day and feels noticeably sharper.
Even a gentle breeze from a fan, brushing my teeth, washing my face, or chewing can trigger a shock immediately.
Staying still, avoiding touching my face, and shielding my cheek from cold drafts help avoid setting it off. Nothing stops it once it strikes.
No, it has never happened on the left side of my face. It is strictly on the right.
No, I visited my dentist last week and had X-rays done, but my teeth and gums were completely healthy.
No, my face does not feel numb or tingling between attacks, and I can feel my cheek normally.
No, both sides of my face move normally, and my smile is not crooked.
No, I have not noticed any rash, bumps, or blisters anywhere on my skin.
I have been feeling quite tired and worn down lately, mostly because the fear of the pain keeps me on edge all day.
No fever, chills, or night sweats at all.
No, I do not have a general headache, and my neck is not stiff.
My vision is totally clear, and I have not had any eye redness, pain, or excessive tearing.
No ear pain, fullness, or hearing loss.
No, my weight has been steady.
I tried taking over-the-counter ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but they did not help the pain at all.
No, I have never experienced anything like this before in my life.
It is making it terrifying to wash my face, shave, or eat, and the anticipation is exhausting.
history.topic: Impact on daily life and sleep

history.answer: I thought it was just a bad toothache or an infected root sending electric jolts through my face.
I'm scared the pain will get so relentless that I won't even be able to eat dinner or talk at work.
I really need something strong right away to stop these awful jolts, and hopefully a referral to figure this out.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or multiple sclerosis.
I have never had any surgeries or stays in the hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only drink occasionally, perhaps one or two beers on social occasions.
I work as an office administrator and live at home with my wife.
No one in my family has had chronic facial pain, nerve disorders, or brain conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-developed man sitting comfortably but looking tense and anxiously protecting the right side of his face from air currents.
No facial skin rash, erythema, swelling, or vesicular lesions are present.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial expressions and intact corneal reflexes bilaterally.
Light touch sensation is intact across all facial distributions, but touching the right nasolabial cheek area triggers a sudden brief electric shock-like jolt.
Dentition is intact without caries, gingival erythema, or tooth tenderness to percussion, and oral mucosa is normal.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light with full extraocular movements and no scleral injection or tearing.
Both external auditory canals and tympanic membranes are clear without inflammation or lesions.
No nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, or Brudzinski sign is present.
